On the Orders of the Day being called:

I wish to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that an answer to a question with regard to freight rates on the Prince Edward Island railway which appeared on the Order Paper yesterday was not printed in ' Hansard.' The only answer that appears in the official report is that the answer had been filed with the Clerk of the House. I should like to know why the invariable rule of the House has been departed from.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I know nothing of the
matter except that the Clerk of the House informs me that the answer consisted of a long series of statistics which it is not usual to print in ' Hansard,' and that the clerk will furnish copies of the answer as may be desired. My hon. friend will remember that there was some discussion about this matter on a previous occasion, and it was stated that the practice which was followed has been pursued for some time.

If the right hon. Prime Minister will pardon me, I do not think there was any previous discussion about this matter; probably it was about a return. It seems to me that the answer to this question should not occupy msre than



a page of ' Hansard.' The object of asking the question was to have the information published.

The rule is
absolute; the answer ought to go on ' Hansard.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not the rule
under my hand at the moment, and I do not know. I do remember that the subject was discussed on a previous occasion, and His Honour the Speaker made some observation with regard to the practice.

Here is the
rule, No. 37:
If a member does not distinguish his question by an asterisk, the minister to whom the question is addressed hands the answer to the Clerk of the House who causes it to be printed in the official report of the Debates.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The practice seems to
me to be growing of late-and it should be more carefully avoided-of putting on the Order Paper questions which require answers containing long lists of figures, and which should more properly be made as a notice of motion. Owing to the desire, 1 suppose, to give the information, these questions are allowed to pass, and their being printed occasions a conflict with the rule which was established some years ago, that nothing should go on ' Hansard ' except what was read in the House-excepting, perhaps, figures given in the Budget Speech, by the Minister of Finance. That rule was laid down, and has been adhered to ever since. It was with reference to questions of this kind that the matter was discussed in the House some time ago, and it was decided then that in such cases, after an exhibit of what was proposed to go into ' Hansard ', the answer should be filed with the Clerk of the House. That was my understanding, and since then I have been endeavouring to follow that rule, although I have given no instructions with regard to questions and answers.

A member has the privilege of putting a question. If the minister thinks that it should stand as an order for a return, he has only so to declare, but if he chooses to answer the question, then the rule provides that the question be handed to the clerk and that the clerk shall put it on ' Hansard.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have not the slightest objection to the answers being printed in full; I understand that the practice which has been observed in this regard was established some years ago. When the 
answer is very long, I agree with my right hon. friend that it would be better for the minister to ask that the question stand as a notice of motion for return.

There seems to be a misapprehension here which should be corrected. The rule provides that answers can be given orally or in writing. Sometimes an answer which is given orally contains a long list of figures, and, the figures not having been read, they should not go into ' Hansard ', but if the member does not ask for an oral answer, and the answer is given in writing, the rule is that the answer shall be given to the clerk, who puts it upon the pages of ' Hansard.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That does seem to be a plain statement of the rule. It is a matter in which I have not interfered in any way whatever, nor has my right hon. friend, as I know. In cases where the answers are long and cumbersome, it would be better in future, I think, for the ministers to let the questions stand as notices of motion. But in cases where that is not done you have the answer printed, as the rule seems to require.
But I suppose when the answer appears the question will also appear in the same 'Hansard' so that it may be intelligible?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly.
On the motion of Mr. White for Committee of Supply:

I wish to call to the attention of the Government and to discuss very briefly the matter of suburban train service in and out of Halifax. It is not, of course, a matter of national importance, but it is of very considerable local interest just at this moment. I have had the advantage of several interviews with the hon. the Minister of Railways on this matter, and I wish to acknowledge his courtesy in this respect; but I feel that the subject is now of such importance that I owe it to my constituents to discuss it here. Between Halifax and Bedford, a distance ol about ten miles, is a well settled suburban district traversed by the Intercolonial railway throughout its entire length. As the Prime Minister knows, this district is located upon Bedford basin, an extension of Halifax harbour, and is an exceedingly popular residential district in the summer season and, to a very large extent in the

winter season as well. It has a permanent population I would say of about one thousand. and in the summer season this is very materially increased, hut to what extent I can hardly estimate-probably by fifty per cent. The residents of this district are people who are largely engaged in business or employed in one manner or another in the city , of Halifax. These people established their residences there upon the assumption that it was the policy of the Intercolonial railway to encourage the growth and development of this suburban district and that it would be continuously provided with suitable train accommodation. Homes have been built there, mercantile businesses have been established, and schools organized upon the assumption that such railway accommodation would obtain. The stability of suburban residences and of mercantile business which are now in existence there, and the prosperity of the district generally is dependent entirely upon the permanence and suitability of the railway service afforded, those who there reside. This is evident, I imagine, to every person who has had any experience in or knowledge of suburban districts. I know that in this particular district at least one industry has been established which employs a considerable amount of labour and I think that its establishment is attributable solely to the fact that it was possible for the labour employed to have ready access to the city of Halifax at hours which were convenient to them. If suitable railway accommodation is not available in suburban districts to the nearest city it is almost impracticable to obtain labour for any industries which might desire to locate there. In connection with suburban districts I think it is generally conceded, and I may predicate it as a fact, that a late night train service is an absolute necessity to its very life and continuance. Suburban dwellers always hope to avail themselves of the amusements and social advantages of city life, and this is only possible with the establishment and maintenance of a late suburban train service. This may sound to some as an extravagant demand on the part of suburban dwellers, but nevertheless it is one of the necessities and advantages demanded, and is one of the inevitable incidents to suburban life.
The district of Bedford has had the advantage of a late night suburban train service to and from Halifax for a long number of years, I believe twenty years; and recently, some two or three weeks ago, this service was summarily discontinued.
The ground alleged for the discontinuance of this railway service, I believe, is that the cost of the service was very much in excess of the revenue derived from it, and consequently the cancellation of this train service is defended upon the ground of economy. I have not had the advantage of seeing any financial statement showing the cost of this service together with its earnings, although the Minister of Railways has promised to furnish me with the same. I wish to submit to the Government that, in my judgment, to determine whether this late train service shall or shall not continue as formerly, upon the net financial result of the operation of this one train is altogether too narrow a view, and the policy should be settled upon broader lines. There are many other things to be considered in determining whether or not this particular train service is financially justifiable. In the first place, it must be very difficult to actually determine whether this service is profitable or not. A great many other trains serve this district incidentally, and many of its residents, and travellers going there, take advantage of these trains; and to this extent returns properly attributable in origin to this suburban district generally can hardly be ascertained with accuracy, and consequently it does not, I fear, receive credit for the same in the calculations of the Railway Department. Again, it is of course obvious that the many residents of this district have many friends, who are obliged to visit there very frequently, and who perhaps do not always avail themselves of what is strictly a suburban railway service, but use other trains, and,	again, any	income derivedfrom	such	travel	can hardly be
accounted for with any precision. The district is further served by another railway, namely, the Dominion Atlantic railway, which uses the Intercolonial rails from Bedford to Halifax. I have no doubt that this railway receives considerable revenue from what is strictly suburban traffic, and that road must account to the Intercolonial for a proportion of the same. It would be very difficult for me to estimate what particular amount is received by the Intercolonial from this same source. Its origin, however, is due to the existence of the suburban district, which was made possible by proper passenger railway accommodation. There is also the question of freight. In this suburban district a freight traffic has grown up. Mercantile establishments have been established to meet the require-

nients of the district, and that necessarily involves considerable freight traffic which inures very much to the benefit of the Intercolonial railway. The value and permanence of this freight traffic is dependent entirely upon the prosperity and growth of this suburban section. If its population decreases the freight traffic will also diminish. Consequently the Intercolonial railway is necessarily interested in the freight traffic, and this must be taken -into consideration in determining the character of the passenger service which Bedford and the intervening district is entitled to.
I have no doubt the Minister of Railways urges in defence of the cancellation of this train service the fact that the rates are too low, and that its re-establishment is only possible by an increase in passenger rates. I submit to the Government that it is the policy of all important railways to encourage suburban settlement. This is sound policy for a great many obvious reasons; and I think it is also the policy of railways, to afford a suburban passenger service at comparatively low commutation. If they are thus successful in developing a prosperous and populous suburban district, there will eventually come a time when the railway traffic of all kinds, originating there, becomes profitable. Therefore, I think I may fairly submit to the Government that that is the policy which should be pursued in this instance by the Intercolonial railway.
As the Prime Minister is no doubt aware, a new passenger arrangement was established and put into operation on Saturday night last, for the convenience of persons resident in the district of Bedford whereby they could leave the city of Halifax at 11.15 p.m. on a passenger car attached to a fast freight train. The result was not very satisfactory and apparently meets with unqualified opposition from those compelled to use it. It took this train one hour and a quarter to travel to Bedford, a distance of 10 miles, and two hours to Windsor Junction, a distance of eighteen or twenty miles. I also understand that the passengers on this train on Saturday last also suffered much discomfort. I do not question the wisdom of the policy which the Minister of Railways in this instance seeks to invoke, namely, to retrench in expenditures on the Intercolonial. That is good business and sound policy, and generally speaking should meet with the commendation of every hon. gentleman in this House. I have pointed out, however, some reasons why the continuance of this suburban night service should not be 
dependent on the contingency of a parity between the cost of the service and its revenue. Other matters, some of which I have mentioned must be taken into consideration. When one looks into the various items of expenditure on the Intercolonial I think it is quite obvious that retrenchment might be made in many other directions. Were it necessary I might suggest many ways to effect proper retrenchments. But in this particular instance I submit it is not necessary to make a retrenchment. Furthermore, the cancellation of this night service at this particular season of the year, and without ample notice to the public, has worked very considerable hardship, as well as great inconvenience and possibly loss. I submit that if such a train service had to be discontinued it should only be upon sufficient notice. The continued cancellation of this train means that a great many people who have established homes in this suburban district will be compelled to give them up. Their residence there is only possible upon the condition that a suitable late night train service is available to them. I know, of my personal knowledge, a number of persons who have settled in that district who," if the present conditions continue, will be obliged to dispose of their property and move into the city of Halifax.
There are many other -reasons which I - might urge for a generous service on the part of the Intercolonial for the residents of this particular district. The scarcity of available homes in the city of Halifax ard the recent enhancement of rents is compelling many people to seriously consider the question of removing their residences to suburban districts. Such are the facts concerning this matter. I have given to the Government my own views upon this matter, and I desire to impress upon them the desirability and necessity of the restoration of the former late night train service from Halifax to Bedford. The present conditions are extremely inconvenient to son e at least, almost intolerable. I believe the district deserves the continuance of the former service, and I do trust that the Minister of Railways or the acting Minister of Railway will see fit to restore this service immediately and without conditions. The reasons assigned for the cancellation are not sound or convincing, and should never have been made, 1 trust that the people interested in the train service may look for an immediate announcement of the resumption of .the abandoned night service. It is quite apparent that the combined passenger and freight service instituted for

the first time on Saturday, will prove ineffective and will hardly provide the remedy. Therefore I trust that the Government will give due and proper consideration to this matter and that we shortly shall have an announcement that a restoration of the service has been authorized.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I received a number of
telegrams this morning from constituents of my own in the city and county of St. -John, and from a number of residents in the adjoining county of Kings, making complaints somewhat similar to those that have been received by my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) from his constituents in Halifax. It is represented to me in these telegrams that the suburban train service, which arrived in St. John at a quarter to eight every morning and left at 6.15 in the evening, was taken off and that it was causing very great inconvenience to a large number of suburban residents who lived along the line of the Intercolonial railway, between St. John and Rothesay and farther east than Rothesay. I fancy that the conditions surrounding the suburban residents near the Kennebecasis river are very similar to those described by my hon. friend outside of Halifax and in the neighbourhood of Bedford Basin. Many people have erected permanent homes for themselves along the line of railway relying upon the regular running of these suburban trains and if these people cannot get to their business at a quarter to eight, or at eight o'clock in the morning, they are put to very great inconvenience and the money that they have invested along the line of railway in permanent homes has to a very considerable extent been spent in vain as they will have to move into the city. The same condition exists at St. John as at Halifax; that is the difficulty of getting residences within the city in which there has been a very considerable growth within the last few years. The railway authorities, I should judge from the telegrams I have received, in place of the suburban train which, for a long time has been arriving in the city at a quarter to eight, have substituted a freight train to which passenger ears are attached. Yesterday morning that train was an hour late and the consequence was that people who live along the line of railway did not get to their places of business at the right time. Some of these were school teachers, others were employed in connection with the telephone exchange and others were merchants, and it is of the utmost importance to them
that they should arrive in the city at a certain time. What they allege is that the train of yesterday morning, the first morning after this change took place, was one hour late, and being a freight train there is grave danger of it being late on many future occasions. A number of concrete instances of inconvenience were brought to my attention. For instance, I am informed that one gentleman who is the principal of a school in St. John had to walk -six miles into the city in consequence of this delay, and that other gentlemen engaged in the telephone and other businesses were placed in a similar unfortunate position. On receipt of this information I immediately communicated with the railway authorities and with the hon. gentleman who is acting as Minister of Railways and brought the facts that had been called to my attention before him, and I received his assurance that the matter will receive immediate attention with the view of remedying any grievance that may exist or any inconvenience to which the people along the line of railway may be put if the facts show that this inconvenience is the result or the change in the suburban service. I feel quite sure that the Railway Department will, without unnecessary delay, take the matter up with the view of finding a remedy for any injustice that may possibly have been done if such a condition should be disclosed upon looking into the facts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate the considerations which have been put forward by my colleague from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) and also the very considerate and moderate way in which he has presented the matter to the attention of the Government. Like himself, I have received representations from people living in Halifax and on Bedford Basin, setting forth the inconvenience which has been occasioned by the change made in the railway arrangements. As has already been pointed out by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), the change was not made in Halifax alone but at various other points, and undoubtedly was made with a view to retrenchment and economical administration. It is quite reasonable that the subject should be considered from the standpoints which, have been put forward by my hon. friend from Halifax. I have learned, as lie has, that the arrangement which commenced on Saturday last has not proved very efficient on the first day of its operation. The subject is under the consideration of the Department of Railways and

Canals. In the pressure of many matters incident to his approaching departure, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) has not within the last day or two been able to give that consideration to the subject which undoubtedly it deserves, but my colleague who will undertake the administration of the department during his absence will give to the subject the very best consideration that may be possible, and I understand that the general manager of the Intercolonial railway is to be here within a day or two, when the subject can be taken up. I am informed that Mr. Gutelius visited Halifax and St. John for the purpose of bringing about some arrangement which would prove reasonably satisfactory to the persons interested. Apparently the arrangement which was made has not proved so reasonably satisfactory as was anticipated by the railway authorities. The observations of my hon. friend from Halifax, and the considerations which he has placed before the Government, will receive very early attention.

We' have the same grievance in the city of Toronto, only on a much larger scale. We have there now half a million of people. We have suburban towns all around Toronto, scores of them, and for years we have been trying to get, as a matter of fact, a suburban service with a commutation ticket. The great city of Montreal, which has now probably 600,000 people, for years has had an excellent suburban service and commutation ticket. Do our best we cannot get that in Toronto, and, as far as I can gather, the railway companies have pleaded that it was an act of grace. I have tried to argue in this House that the railway should give it as a matter of law and equity, and I hope that in the revision of the Railway Act it will be clearly set out that a city which establishes a right to a suburban service and to a commutation ticket will be entitled to them. No one can quite understand how serious this condition is in Toronto. We have a congestion in street car traffic every night and every morning that is almost unbearable. People cannot get out to the suburbs. It often takes a man an hour to get to his suburban home. The population of any constituency of South York, which was less than 25,000 at the last redistribution, is now over
100,000,	and nearly all these people can get to their homes over a. suburban railway

connected with the steam railways. The railway companies have deliberately adopted the policy that it is not their business to supply this service, but that this duty lies with the radial and the street railway companies. That may be true, but inasmuch as those railways are for the general convenience of the public and the public have contributed largely to their support, where a suburban service is called for, it ought to be given. The experiment certainly ought to be tried, and if it is found that it is not of a selfsustaining character it can be cancelled. But the right to try the experiment ought to be secured to the public in the general Railway Act. That is one of the questions that I propose to bring up in connection with the revision of that Act. Certainly the city of Toronto is to-day very much in need of such a service. Montreal has it and it has been proved to be profitable there. I think it would be profitable in Toronto, and in that way the people would be very well served by the steam railway where this condition of affairs exists. I quite admit that a railway company is not bound to give a suburban service where it may be unprofitable. If it were given in one city, the right to have it might be claimed in a great many cities. In large centres of population, however, the steam roads ought to be compelled, when the necessity arises, to serve the people, especially when the traffic can be shown to be profitable. That certainly is the case in Toronto and it may be the case in Halifax and St. John. If it is, the cities on the Intercolonial railway ought to have some kind of suburban service. As far as the other roads are concerned, in the large cities we ought to have the right to demand a suburban service with a commutation rate.

On motion of Mr. White for Committee of Supply:
Hon. OHAS. MARCEL: I want to draw attention to what I consider is an oversight on the part of the members of the Commission on Internal Economy. I refer to the case of the late Napoleon Jallet, permanent sessional messenger of this House, who died on the opening day of last session. His widow called on me yesterday to remind me that nothing had been done in her behalf. Her husband was from Montreal, and I had known him for fourteen or fifteen years. He had the distinc-

tion of being in the service of the House for forty-seven years without interruption, having been appointed in 1866. During that time he gave faithful service. For fifteen years he was special messenger to the Deputy Speakers of this House. By some oversight nothing has been done for the widow. I think I spoke to your honour, Mr. Speaker, about this matter last year.
I hope the mention of it now will be sufficient to ensure that something will be done for her.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I remember the hon.
member speaking about this matter. I made a memorandum of it at the time and looked into it, and I believe that a resolution was passed by the Commission on Internal Economy, but that it was accidentally overlooked. I shall be glad to look into the matter.
On the motion of Mr. White for Committee of Supply:

I would like to deal with a matter of considerable importance to the western provinces. This House is familiar with the fact that the policy of the present Prime Minister, the leader of the Opposition in 1905, was favourable to the transfer to the western provinces of their natural resources. That policy was adhered to during the campaign of 1911, and I desire to ascertain from, the Prime Minister to-day whether it is the intention of the Government to transfer to the western provinces their natural resources, as promised by himself in many public declarations throughout western Canada, as promised on the Halifax platform and as prominently mentioned in the Conservatives' handbook which was freely distributed throughout the country during the 1911 campaign.
It has been said that, on account of the fact that certain of the provinces of western Canada have returned Liberal governments to administer their affairs, this policy of the Prime Minister has not been acceptable to the people of the West. I do not think that argument holds water, for this reason, that ever since the first elections in 1905 and the elections of 1909 in the provinces of the West the Prime Minister 4 p.m. has adhered to that part of his platform in regard to the return to the western provinces of their natural resources. In the 1911 campaign this was
one of the arguments used to offset the strong sentiment in favour of reciprocity in the prairie provinces. I had very much pleasure in listening to the Prime Minister during his visit to Lethbridge in 1911.	He referred to the matter of natural resources, and I was led to believe that if the then leader of the Opposition was returned to power, within a very few months these natural resources would be handed over to the province of Alberta and also to the province of Saskatchewan. There was no statement that these natural resources would not be handed over until there was a Conservative Government in the province of Alberta and a Conservative Government in the province of Saskatchewan. The statement was boldly made that the Conservative party in this country were in favour of the natural resources being placed in the possession of the provinces, and that if that party were returned to power, at the first opportunity that part of their platform would be carried out. It is in regard to the failure of the Government to carry out that policy that I desire to draw the attention of the House to-day.
I would like to refer to some of the statements made by the Prime Minister at the time when he was leader of the Opposition and during his visit to western Canada in 1911. At Brandon, in 1911, at the commencement of his tour through western Canada, the then leader of the Opposition said:	.
In 1902, in 1905, in 1907, ana again in 1910, we have stood for the right of the western provinces to own and control their public domain. It is the right of the people in those provinces to have their public lands and natural resources administered by their own governments under the control of their own legislatures. They say that they are free men and being free men in a free country have as good a right to control through their own local legislatures, and by their own provincial executives, the administration of their public lands and natural resources as have the people of any of the eastern provinces who enjoy and have enjoyed that right. The Liberal-Conservative party supports that claim and will enforce it at the first opportunity.
The ' first opportunity ' came at the end of 1911. That opportunity has existed during the years 1912 and 1913, and exists at the present time. The-people of the West, believing that the Prime Minister was in earnest in the promise which he made to them naturally expect him to carry out his policy, even though the West is not returning to his support a majority of its members, or even though some of the western provinces are not supporting a

Conservative Government, because there was no stipulation that these resources would be handed over only when the Conservative party was in power in the western provinces.
Further, in regard to the platform pledges of the leader of the Conservative party in the 1911 campaign, I would like to quote what he stated at Battleford in order to show his insincerity. This is what he said:
If it should be the w.ll of the people of Canada to impose upon me the great responsibility of being called upon to form a government in Canada and after that government has been formed, the policy I have outlined will be carried out by the government as I have stated, or one man of the government will go out of public life.
These were very striking and very important statements. I always had a very high conception of the then leader of the Opposition. I believed that he was sincere in his attitude on public questions. I was not so narrow a partisan as to believe that if the then leader of the Opposition was returned to lead a government in this country, he would fail to carry out his promises. I was of the opinion that he would carry out his promises as promptly as he could. Instead of that, the Prime Minister of this country is departing from the policy which he had in 1905 and in 1911. because we find that when the boundaries of Manitoba were extended the idea of giving the provinces their natural resources was to a greater or less extent abandoned. But early in the session of 1911, the Prime Minister was queried by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) in regard to this matter, and it appeared to me then that he was still of the opinion that the provinces should have control of their natural resources. The following are the questions put by the hon. member for Regina, with the answers given by the Prime Minister:
Mr. Martin (Regina) :
1.	Is the Government aware that the present Prime Minister during the last election promised to favour a policy of handing over to the western provinces their natural resources?
2.	If so, what steps does the Government intend to take toward implementing such promise?
Mr. Borden:
1.	Yes.
2.	The steps will be announced in Parliament in due course.
This Parliament is running very rapidly to its expiration, and it is about time the Prime Minister declared whether he is going to carry out the policy which he announced in 1911, a policy which he stood 
for then in the western provinces and which he said unequivocally he would carry out at the first opportunity. I would like to point out to the Prime Minister this fact -though, of course, I do not say that he is back of the actions of his followers in western Canada-that in the two provincial general elections held in the West since this Government was returned to power, one in Saskatchewan and one in Alberta, the argument was used by leaders of the Conservative party, and also in the press of the party, that these provinces could not expect to be given control of their natural resources until the Conservative party was returned to power in those provinces. I do not remember that the Prime Minister made such a stipulation, but that was the argument that was used on the occasions to which I have referred. And it was used as a bribe to the electors of these provinces in direct violation of that part of the Halifax platform opposed to electoral corruption. The argument was used with the same intention as if the man who used it had gone out and offered money to bribe the electors. They told the people that they could not have their natural resources, though that had been promised them, unless they returned Conservative governments to power in Alberta and Saskatchewan. The Prime Minister, holding the high ideals on public questions to which he has given expression, should note these facts. I draw to his attention these arguments which are used by his followers in western Canada.
Now, I have become an admirer of the independence of my fellow representative from the province of Alberta, the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett). He is a representative of a certain type of western sentiment, which is independent enough to speak out plainly. I remember reading, and being very much impressed by, the remarks made by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) on the occasion of the annual meeting of his electors which it is his custom to hold. And it is a very good idea: The member gathers the electors together, and they fill the largest hall in Calgary, and he makes a statement covering the work of the session and the record of the Government. Of course, as this matter of natural resources is vital to the people of the West on account of the promise made in regard to it, I would like to quote from a paper friendly to the hon. member for Calgary, in fact his warm admirer, the Calgary News-Telegram, a report of the hon. gentleman's statement on that point:

He declared that Mr. Borden would keep his promise to restore these resources to the people and the province, and that it the Conservative Premier failed to keep his pledge he would no longer feel bound to give his support to the present Government.
That, I believe, a great many people in the West thought a bold declaration. I bring this remark to the attention of the Prime Minister. It represents a sentiment that, I believe, is widely entertained by independent-minded Conservatives of the province of Alberta. It may not exist among the machine men of the party, who are trying to use the natural resources as a bribe at every election, but it does exist amongst independent-minded Conservatives who wish to see the Prime Minister carry out his promise in this regard. Now, the statement is made that the Prime Minister will convey these resources to the people of the provinces, and the hon. member for Calgary says that if that is not done he will withdraw his support from the Conservative party. But I assume that he is hopeful that the natural resources will be returned to the people of Alberta. I would like some enlightenment on this matter. I should be very glad to welcome the hon. member for Calgary to this side of the House because he had lost faith in the other side, but at the same time, I want a declaration from the Prime Minister in regard to this matter. I think I can say this for the people of the West-that they are sincere, and they expect public men and governments to be sincere. Therefore they look to the Prime Minister to carry out the promises he made in 1911 and prior to that time. This demand for the provincial control of natural resources was recently made by the Premiers of the three western provinces-not only the Premiers of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, in which there are Liberal governments, but also by the Premier of Manitoba, Sir Rodmond Roblin. In a letter to the Prime Minister of the Dominion, these Premiers say:
December 22, 1913. The Rt. Hon. R. L. Borden,
Prime Minister,
. Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-After having an interview with you in regard to the questions in respect of which the prairie provinces received different treatment from the other provinces of Canada, and, at your suggestion, a meeting of the Premiers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta was held, and it has been agreed between us to make to you on behalf of said provinces the proposal that the financial terms already arranged between the provinces and the Dominion as compensation for lands should stand as compensation for lands already alienated for the general benefit of Canada, and, that all the lands remaining within the boundaries of the respective provinces with all natural resources included, be transferred to the said provinces, the provinces accepting responsibility of administering the same.
Yours very truly,
R. P. Rohlin,
Walter Scott.
Arthur B. Sifton. . The Rt. Hon. R. L. Borden,
Prime Minister, Ottawa.
I have placed this matter as briefly as I-could before the House, and I ask a statement from the Prime Minister, in order that the people of the West may be informed as to this very important plank of the platform of 1911. In passing, I may say that, as the Dominion Government controls the natural resources of the western provinces, during this session I had occasion to ask a question regarding the exportation of natural gas from the province of Alberta. People in my constituency are very anxious that none of the gas should be exported from Medicine Hat and Bow Island gas fields, as they wish to conserve that very great and very valuable asset. I asked the question whether this Government had the power to prevent the export of this gas from Alberta into Saskatchewan.
I was told that there were no regulations which the Government could utilize to prevent the exportation of gas from Alberta to Saskatchewan. If the Prime Minister had carried out his promise to transfer the natural resources to the province of Alberta, there would have been no question about the exportation of natural gas. The power would be in the hands of the provincial Government, and they would see that the gas was not allowed to leave the province, thus protecting the interests of those communities which are so anxious, for their welfare as industrial centres, that the supply of gas shall not be used outside the province, or, to any great extent, outside the district of production.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is
quite within his rights in asking for a statement from the Government respecting this matter, and I have no exception to take to the way in which he has presented it, excepting some suggestions he made as to insincerity, with regard to which it might be well for him to take a look at himself and his friends in the West. If I am not mistaken, my hon. friend was one of those who strongly advocated the retention of these lands by Canada at the time

the new provinces were constituted. More than that, my hon. friend was one of those who argued, and stoutly argued, that the financial terms made with these provinces in consideration of the retention of those lands by Canada were far more in the interests of those provinces than would have been the transfer of those natural resources at that time. Therefore, before my hon. friend begins to throw taunts of that kind across the floor of this House, it would be well for him to explain how it is that, entertaining, and I presume, sincerely entertaining the views which he expressed at that time, he has now come to so marvellous a change of heart, and is impressed with the idea that the proposals for which I fought when he opposed them in 1905 are so much in the interest of the people of the western provinces. It was myself and my friends here in the House of Commons in 1905 who urged that the natural resources of the western provinces should fee handed over at that time, and if the course which we then advocated had been carried out by the Government of the day, which the hon. gentleman then supported in that respect as well as in other respects, the difficulties which now have to be surmounted before those natural resources can be transferred to the western provinces would not present themselves to Parliament and to the Government to-day.
Since my hon. friend is desirous of considering the question of sincerity, perhaps it is well that we should take a little review of this matter. Let us look for a moment to the attitude which the Government of the day and my hon. friend who . has just addressed the House adopted in 1905. The then Prime Minister said this:
It was represented that as a matter of law and equity the public lands in these two provinces should belong to their governments. This plea was no doubt suggested by the fact that, at the time of confederation, all parties to the original contract, that is to say, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario, each retained her own lands, and when at a later day the province of British Columbia was admitted to the Dominion, she also retained her lands.. But, Sir, the cases are not at ail parallel. When the provinces which I have named came into confederation they were already sovereignties.
Further on, he said this:
Those lands were bought by the Dominion Government and they have remained ever since the property of the Dominion Government and have been administered by the Dominion Government. Therefore, I say the two cases are not in any way parallel; they are indeed absolutely different. When the provinces which I have name came into consideration they retained the ownership of their lands; but when the two new provinces came into the Do-[Mr. Borden. 1
minion, it cannot be said that they can retain the ownership of their lands, as they never had the ownership.
Then, speaking of what was done on a previous occasion by the Liberal-Conservative Government, the then Prime Minister said that the reasons which bad in fluenced the course of the Government at that time were stronger in 1905 than they were in 1884. He admitted that the provinces, being deprived of public lands, were deprived of a valuable source of income, and he said that it was therefore the duty of Parliament to make ample and generous provision in the way of compensation. My hon. friend the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) took the same if not a stronger attitude with regard to the matter in 1903, when he used this language:
It is of no advantage to the people of the territories that they should be permitted to sell the lands of the territories. If they sell the lands, settlement is thereby deterred; if they do not sell them, they derive no revenue from them, and in so far as that is concerned they might as well be administered by the Dominion Government as by themselves.
The Minister of the Interior of that day laid down the policy of his party, and I understand that my hon. friend the member for Medicine Hat strongly supported this view at that time. He has given us no explanation whatever of the change of heart which he has since experienced. The Minister of Interior of that day used this language:
If you hand over the lands to three provincial governments-because you would have to treat Manitoba in the same way that you are treating the territories-if you hand over the lands to three separate provincial governments, each with its own ideas of policy, each with its own minister of Crown lands, and if the federal Government has to deal with three provincial governments, every man who knows anything about doing business between governments must know that it would he absolutely impossible that satisfactory results could be achieved.
Further on, in the course of the same speech, he used this language:
It might he, Mr. Speaker, and probably would be, that instead of administering these lands for the purpose of . settlement they would administer them for the purpose of revenue, and I do not know that we could blame them very much if they did so. But if they did that, the result would be that the settlement policy of the country would stop.
In conclusion, he added these words:
I would say that nothing could be done which would more certainly imperil the successful settlement policy upon which the greatness and increase in the financial strength and
ressources of Canada depend, than under any

circumstances to allow the public lands of the prairie provinces to pass from the control of the Dominion Government.
I have placed these extracts before the House in order to make it plain to my hon. friend the member for Medicine Hat that a certain policy which he then supported was put forward very strongly in this House by the gentlemen who then held the reins of government. It is perfectly true, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat has said, that we stood at that time for the opposite policy, and declared in Parliament, both by speech and by resolution, that it would be a desirable thing to hand over the natural resources of the western provinces to the control and administration of the people and governments of those provinces when they were established.
After the provinces were constituted and established, an election was held, and the terms of the constitutional Act which forms the charters of those provinces were placed before the people; and at that election and at several subsequent elections it Ans claimed by the Governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta that the people had ratified, over and over again, the terms in respect of their natural resources which were contained in the Alberta Act and in the Saskatchewan Act. It might not be without interest that I should state very briefly the attitude which has been assumed from time to time by the leaders of the Liberal party in the western provinces on this question. I observe that in 1908 the present Prime Minister of the province of Saskatchewan said this:
In addition to the Parliament of Canada having settled the question, the province has settled it in the campaign of 1005. It was plainly put and fully discussed. He was satisfied that the cash grant which the provinces obtained in lieu of their public domain was more advantageous to them than the lands would he.
Speaking at Regina, on August 15, 1908, Hon. Mr. Scott said:
We have heard a great deal about the land issue. As I pointed out in this hall on Wednesday evening, in regard to the verdict the people gave three years ago on the land as well as other autonomy questions, what was there' for the Government to do hut what we have done. The people did not want the land arrangement disturbed. They said the same yesterday. How long is it going to take the people of Saskatchewan to convince Mr. Haultain that they are satisfied with the terms granted them by the Autonomy Act?
And so on through a great number of quotations which I could place before the House if it were desirable to do so. Finally in 1910, on the 6th of October, the Prime Minister of Saskatchewan used this language:
Am I going too far when I suggest a doubt as to the sanity of any Saskatchewan man who complains against our land terms?
It could hardly be put much more strongly than that.
Now, let us see what the subsequent attitude has been. There was a resolution of the Saskatchewan Legislature when first the leaders of the Liberal party in the West began	to withdraw a little from the position which they at first had assumed in this respect. A resolution was adopted by the Legislature of Saskatchewan which is set forth in the question put by the hon. member for Regina to which the hon. member for Medicine Hat has alluded. The operative part of the resolution is this:
Whereas the said northern part of the province of Saskatchewan is not required by the Government of Canada for the purposes of carrying out its colonization and immigration policy.
And whereas, in addition to the agricultural lands there are certain natural resources within Saskatchewan which are purely of local concern and which are not required by the federal authorities for the carrying out of its colonization policy.	.
Therefore it is resolved that, in the opinion of this House, the Government of Saskatchewan should proceed with negotiations with the federal authorities for the purpose of having transferred to the province all that part of the hinterland of Saskatchewan, together with all natural resources of purely local concern contained within the province, not required for colonization and immigration purposes.
That was passed by the Legislature of Saskatchewan on the 16th day of March, 1911, and that is as far, according to my information on the subject, as the Legislature of either Saskatchewan or Alberta had advanced up to the time that the present federal Government assumed the reins of office.
Now, after we had come into office this question was at once pressed upon us, and the advance of Liberal sentiment in the west of Canada has been very marked on this subject. In the first place western Liberals declared over and over again that the terms contained in the Alberta Act and in the Saskatchewan Act were much more advantageous to those provinces than the transfer of the natural resources. In the next place, they declared that the question had been settled over and over again by the people of those provinces; and, further than that, they declared that any man might justly be regarded as

insane who would seek to disturb that arrangement. Then, advancing from that, they came to the conclusion that in each province there might be a portion but not the whole of the natural resources of the province transferred to the ownership and control of the province. Finally, after we had attained office, a very rapid advance was made, and they asked that all the natural resources of the prov, inee should be transferred to them; and during the last year or eighteen months they have made a still further rapid advance and have asked not only that all the natural resources of the province should be transferred to them but that they should retain the grant made out of the federal treasury of Canada, as compensation for the natural resources. When my hon. friend suggests that there has been any change of attitude on the part of the present Administration, might I respectfully ask that he would turn his introspection upon the consideration of these kaleidoscopic changes and inform us what is the reason which has impelled this very rapid development and advance of policy in the Liberal leaders of the West?
I said to the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin), when he asked me a question in this House either last session or the session before, that we were standing upon this question exactly where we stood in 1905. The very declaration to which attention was then called, a declaration made in the Halifax platform of 1907, was this:
The restoration of the public lands to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan upon fair terms.
And it was my hope and desire that when there was a conference between the Premiers of all the provinces of Canada during last autumn this subject would have been taken up and discussed at that conference, because every one knew that the question of the rights of the Maritime provinces in connection with the transfer of these natural resources to the western provinces had been made the subject of debate in this House. My hon. friend the member for the city of St. John ^ (Mr. Pugsley) had, indeed urged this subject upon my attention in the session of 1912; and I said at that time what I hold to-day with regard to the whole subject. Mr. Pugsley asked me at that time, in connection with the Ontario boundary question and in connection, if I remember correctly, with the transfer of their resources to the western provinces, whether the position of the smaller provinces-Nova 
Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island-with regard to financial considerations would not receive attention. It was pointed out on behalf of the Maritime provinces at that time that being members of this Confederation they had certain rights in connection with lands that had been acquired by Canada in the first instance, and they also had certain rights by reason of the fact that Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba had had their boundaries very greatly extended and that there was no similar opportunity for the people of the Maritime provinces to have their boundaries extended. I said, in reply to the observations of the hon. member for St. John:
I quite appreciate the spirit and the object of the observations that my hon. friend has just submitted. I have not the slightest hesitation in saying to him what I have said very distinctly before, that the views he put forward do appeal to me, and I think, that in regard to the territory of these two very large provinces and in connection with the proposed transfer of the public domain to the three prairie provinces, the just rights of the Maritime provinces of .Canada must be taken into consideration.
And I had hoped that that subject would have been taken into consideration by the representatives of the governments of the various provinces; but apparently that was not done, and the subject remains for the consideration of this Government, and later, no doubt, for the consideration of Parliament.
A very important letter upon this subject was addressed by the Premier of Alberta to my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition, on the 20th day of March, 1911, and I propose, for the information of the House, to place some extracts from that letter upon the pages of Hansard. At a later date I propose to have all the documents in connection with this matter brought down in the form of a blue book so that they will be available to hon. members of this House. The letter from Mr. Sifton to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, under date of the 20th March, is very long. It sets forth many reasons urged by Mr. Sifton upon Sir Wilfrid Laurier for the transfer of a portion of the natural resources of the prairie provinces to the governments of those provinces. That portion of the letter which contains his claim is in these words:
Therefore, with these observations in mind, acting in accordance with the resolution of the Legislative Assembly of Alberta, and believing that the request following will promote the good government and advancement of the province of Alberta without conflicting with the wider interests of the Dominion of Canada, the Gov-

eminent of the province respectfully asks your Government to grant the measure of control of the natural resources of the province as generally stated in the following request, and express the desire that your Government will take the matter into consideration and give effect to our claim:
1.	That the administration for the beneficial use of the province of all lands belonging to the Crown situated in the province of Alberta be transferred to the province, except the following :
(a)	Lands reserved by statute or Order in Council.
(b)	Lands reserved for Indians.
(c)	Lands earned by any person or corporation.
(d)	Lands agreed upon as homestead or preemption lands, etc.
In essence this means the grazing lands, swamp lands, and the lands that require to be irrigated.
2.	That all mines, minerals, timber and royalties belonging to the Crown situated in the province of Alberta, and all sums due in respect thereof on a date to be fixed by agreement, be transferred to the province of Alberta.
3.	That the interest of the Crown in the waters within the province under the Irrigation Act be vested in and administered by the province of Alberta.
No reply seems to have been given to that letter until the 7th of the following August, when Sir Wilfrid wrote a letter to Mr. Sifton from which I abstract the essential and relevant part of the answer:
I do not understand you to claim that the province of Alberta should be given the ownership or the administration of all the public domain in that province, but simply of the lands which are not solely agricultural. You recognize that the Dominion should continue to own and to administer the prairie lands which are immediately available for settlement and which are sought by the immigrants; but you ask that the province should be entrusted with the ownership and administration of all other lands and all the resources to be derived therefrom, viz., grazing lands, swamp lands, lands unfit for settlement except by irrigation, all the mines, timber, minerals and royalties belonging to the Crown, and all the waters now included in the Irrigation Act.
I have to observe that your proposition, if accepted, would constitute a material alteration of the basis on which the financial terms granted to the province were calculated, and that consequently those financial terms would have to be revised.
This material consequence being kept in mind, the request of the Legislature of Alberta might constitute a fair subject of discussion, without however, at this early juncture, committing ourselves to the acceptance of the principle involved.
The House will appreciate the fact that at that time the province of Alberta did not ask for the whole of its natural resources, but for only a very limited portion of them, and the reply of my hon. friend's leader was this:
I have to observe that your proposition, if accepted, would constitute a material alteration of the basis on which the financial terms granted to the province were calculated, and that consequently those financial terms would have to be revised.
My hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) is astonished now, notwithstanding that declaration of his leader, of which he cannot be ignorant, because we have not handed over all the natural resources of those provinces to the control of their Governments without any revision whatever of the financial terms which were established by their constitutional Acts. It would have been well for my hon. friend the member for Medicine Hat, before making some of the suggestions which fell from him in the course of the debate, to have given .some consideration to the words and attitude of his own leader in that regard; and I must say that I do not see how it is possible for him to suggest to us now, in respect to a province whieh by its accredited representatives elected by the people, has stated over and over again that the terms contained in its constitutional Act were not only fair but better than the actual transfer of the lands themselves-I do not see how it is possible for him to suggest that we should hand over those natural resources, and leave the province to enjoy the very terms which were inserted in its constitutional Act as a consideration for the retention of those natural resources by the Government of Canada.
It is perfectly true that the subject was discussed between three Prime Ministers of the western provinces and myself about the time of the conclusion of the Interprovincial Conference. We had a very amicable discussion of the subject, and at the end of the conference I suggested that if they had any proposal to make to the Government with regard to the terms which I said was a very material matter to be considered, I would be glad to have them submit their suggestions to me in writing, and I would give them immediate consideration. In reply to that, I received towards the end of December, 1913, a letter from the Hon. Arthur L. Sifton in the following terms:
Dear Mr. Borden:
Inclosed please find letter on land question, signed by the premiers of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta.
Hoping that the question may receive early consideration, I am,
Yours very truly
(Sgd) Arthur L. Sifton.

The letter enclosed is in these terms:
After having an interview with you in rfegard to the questions in respect of which the prairie provinces have received different treatment from the other provinces of Canada, and at your suggestion a meeting of the premiers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, it has been agreed between us to make to you, on behalf of said province, the proposal that the financial terms already arranged between the provinces and the Dominion as compensation for lands should stand as compensation for lands already alienated for the general benefit of Canada, and that all the lands remaining within the' boundaries of the respective provinces, with all natural resources included, be transferred to the said province, the provinces accepting respectively the responsibility of administering the same.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd) Walter Scott,
" R. P. Roblin.
" Arthur D. Slfton. The Rt. Hon. R. T,. Borden,
Prime Minister, Ottawa.
This letter called for the transfer to the three western provinces of all the natural resources, without any abatement or revision of the sum which had been fixed in 1905 as compensation for those lands and which sum had been declared over and over again by the Liberal leaders of the West to be more than ample compensation for those lands. Only the session before this, if I remember correctly, we had taken back the swamp lands of Manitoba and thus the Government of Canada became seized of all the natural resources within the province of Manitoba, as it was seized of all the natural resources within the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan; and we made very considerable additions to the amounts receivable by the province of Manitoba out of the federal treasury by reason of the arrangement made at that time. Under these circumstances I could not regard the proposal put forward to me by the three premiers as a reasonable proposal or as containing anything in the nature of those terms which I had asked them to place before me at the conference to which I have alluded. In view of what had been said in Parliament, in view of the declarations which I myself, bad made in Parliament, I thought it advisable, as the subject had not been under discussion at the Interprovincial Conference, to place this communication before the governments of the three Maritime provinces, and I did so.
I wrote on the 8th of January, 1914, shortly after I had received this letter, to the Hon. George H. Murray, Premier of Nova Scotia :

Two or three weeks afterwards I received a letter from Mr. Murray under date of the 19th of January, which I shall take the liberty of reading to the House:
Halifax, January 19, 1914.
Dear Sir,-In further reply to your letter of the 8th instant, enclosing copy of a letter received by you from the Prime Ministers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, on the subject of the transfer of federal lands to the said provinces, I regret that I have not had an opportunity of reading the discussions which occurred in the House of Commons when the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were created. I know that the land question was very fully discussed and I think it was in connection with the enactment of the provincial constitutions.
The question first came up when the province of Manitoba was created. The same argument that was used later in the case of the other provinces was brought forward in support of a proposal to give Manitoba land. Sir John Macdonald took strong ground against it, making the particular point that in western Canada the land question was closely associated with the question of immigration and that therefore the Dominion, which had to spend so liberally for immigration, should have control of the lands. It is apparent that the Government of Sir Wilfrid Daurier took the same view in the case of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I know that when the two new provinces were created the federal Government dealt very liberally with them in respect to financial matters. In comparison with the financial terms given to the Maritime provinces the financial arrangement seemed very generous and I always understood that the large annual grants

107&
of money were by reason of the fact that the western provinces did not get the lands. My recollection is that they got their generous subsidy in two distinct forms:
A portion for general subsidy and another portion specifically in lieu of lands. If this be the case it would look somewhat unreasonable for these provinces to ask, in view of the great financial difficulties of some of the other provinces, for both lands and the money. But I recognize the fact that the question of the wisdom of giving the provinces the lands is one between the Dominion Government and the western provinces and one on which I do not understand I am called to express an opinion, as this is a matter for adjustment between the western provincial Government and the Ottawa Cabinet. I desire, however, to respectfully point out to you;
(1)	That when it was deemed expedient to retain the lands in the control of the Dominion Government this was the consideration for a substantial money allowance being made to the provinces in lieu of these lands;
(2)	That the whole financial arrangement for the western provinces appears to have been made in a fair and generous spirit so that these provinces, in my opinion, do not appear to have any ground for financial complaint as to their treatment in comparison with the other provinces of the Dominion. In fact, I think I can present an almost unanswerable case in the other direction.
(3)	That if the allowances in lieu of land was. when made, fair and reasonable (as to which there does not appear to^have been any question) it certainly cannot be far an 1 reasonable for these provinces now to ask for both the lands and the money which was paid them in lieu of lands. The adoption of such a proposal by the federal Government would be an entire disturbance of the financial arrangement between the various provinces and calculated to produce wide-spread discontent.
(4) That if in the interests of any of the provinces it be deemed expedient to make further	grants from	the Dominion Treasury for provincial purposes, such action should only be taken as part of a general readjustment of financial arrangements in which all the provinces should have an opportunity to participate. If the needs of the western provinces call for additional financial grants (and I have no doubt such is the case) either by giving lands or better financial terms, I do not take the ground that their case should not be considered but I do, in justice to the other provinces, urge that their claims be inquired into and dealt with at the same time.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd) G. H. Murray, The Right Honourable R. L. Borden,

Premier's office.
Charlottetown, February 2, 1914.
Re claim of Alberta. Saskatchewan and Manitoba to federal lands within their borders.
Dear Mr. Borden,-In reply to your letter of the 8th ultimo. I beg to say:
1.	That the grant to Alberta and Saskatchewan of $375,000 increasing to $1,125,000 each per annum as compensation for public lands was an allowance far exceeding in generosity any subsidy to the older provinces.
2.	That in 1912 Manitoba made restitution to Canada in respect of the federal lands granted to that province in order to receive in lieu thereof the exceedingly favourable terms granted to Alberta and Saskatchewan.
3.	That the claim of these provinces to retain their land subsidy as compensation for lands disposed of by the Dominion before they were established as (provinces is not well founded, because the Dom nion Government:
(a)	Bore the whole cost of development since these territories were acquired by Canada and established the new provinces free of debt.
(b)	Paid these provinces an annual subsidy on account of their having no debt.
(c)	The self-governing colonies had to furnish for themselves the public works and services which Canada provided for the territories before establishing them as provinces, and where the colonies had to borrow money for the purpose, it was afterwards charged against them on balancing the debt accounts between them and Canada.
4.	That if the subsidy for want of land is continued and the lands also granted to these provinces, it would give rise to a new or additional claim for compensation from every other province in Canada.
Faithfully yours,
(Sgd) J. A. Mathieson.

Premier's office,
Woodstock, N.B., Peb. 17, 1914. The Right Hon. R. L. Borden,
Prime Minister,
Ottawa, Canada,
My Dear Prime Minister,-Some time ago you sent me a copy of letter received from the Premiers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta in regard to the control of the federal lands within the boundaries of these three provinces.
In connection with this subject the interests of the Maritime provinces are peculiarly and particularly affected. I believe the financial arrangements between the federal Government and three .western provinces were made having in view the fact that the federal Government was retaining the public lands within the three provinces, and a large amount was allowed them annually on this account. Such being the case, I do not think they have any just or reasonable claim to ask for the federal lands.
As to the wisdom of these three prairie provinces having handed over to them the public lands is a question between the federal Government and the provinces interested and affected, and I do not wish to express any opinion in relation to that question.
I wish to remind your Administration of the fact that in February of last year representatives on behalf of the Maritime provinces put forward claims for compensation on account of alienation of federal lands, the cases considered at that time being the large addition made to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario by Act of Parliament, and the provision in the western provinces in connection with what was known as the school lands.
The immense area of the public domain north of Quebec, north of Ontario and on the western prairies is our common property. It may be wise public policy to cede these lands to the provinces, and I do not dissent from it being done, but I cannot believe it would be right to do so without some compensation being made to the Maritime provinces, whose geographical position is such that they can receive no territorial expansion.
Tours sincerely,
(Sgd)'J. K. Flemming.
My hon. friend from Medicine Hat will observe that in the utterance of the 7th of August, 1911, which was communicated to the Hon. A. L. Sifton, Premier of Alberta, it was distinctly stated as the policy of the party of which my hon. friend from Medicine Hat is a supporter, that the transfer of the natural resources to the provinces could not be made nor could the proposal be entertained without consideration and revision of the financial arrangements which were established as compensation for those lands. He will also observe that the three provincial Premiers who claim to have some special interest on behalf of their provinces in this sub-
