So, this bulletin, issued for the purpose . of informing the people-misinforming them rather-as to what the present minister is doing is set down the same inaccuracy- they set down the figures of agriculture with $700,000 duplicated. Some explanation seems called for concerning the putting into the hands of the public such an irresponsible publication as this. The whole of this magazine, taking it from the first page to the last, contains inaccuracies quite as glaring and indefensible.
Will the hon. gentleman please point out some more of them?

Yes, I can point out more. In a ' foreword ' over the signature of the minister, this appears:
The magazine is designed ... to supply to the press and to those who are engaged in agricultural work, facts and information relating to the educational and scientific side of agriculture.
But here on page 6 is a statement that the Hon. Frangois Evanturel was the first Minister of Agriculture. The fact is that

the first Minister of Agriculture was the Hon. N. F. Belleau, in 1862. At page 10, under the special heading ' Exhibition * Branch ' the magazine speaks of the World's Centennial Exhibition in 1876, and then jumps to the Pan-American in 1901. No leference is made to the Paris Exposition of 1878; Antwerp, 1885; Colonial and Indian Exposition, 1886; Liverpool, Royal Jubilee Exposition, 1887; Doncaster, Royal Agricultural Society, 1891; Chicago World's Columbian Exposition, 1893; Antwerp, 1894; Stockholm, 1897; Omaha, 1898; Paris, 1900; Glasgow, Scotland, 1901. At page 17, there is a list of experimental farms up to date. But it is interesting to note that the dates of their establishment are not shown. Were they shown it would be seen that all these farms except three were established by the late Minister of Agriculture. It is perfectly obvious why the dates are not given. With regard to the expenditures by the late Government under the head of ' Civil Government ' an expenditure of $1,200 is omitted in 1900. In the matter of experimental farms-
Before the hon. gentleman leaves that point would he be good enough to state what experimental farms were established by the late Government?
I should- be able to state it if this magazine contained the information, but as it does not contain it and I have no other authority at hand, I am not in a position to give the names.

I understood the hon.
gentleman to say that all but three were established by the former Administration.
I do not think he is quite correct.
'Mr. J. J. HUGHES: The statement made was that there were only three established by this Government.

With regard to the figures of expenditure, I was about to say that an item of $8,000 appropriated for experimental farms is omitted from the figures of 1900. The items for dairying and cold storage omit a sum of $20,000. The whole vote for health of animals amounting in 1900 under the late Government to $65,000 is omitted, as also is an item of $1,600 for fumigation stations. In the Estimates of 1904-5 there were appropriations under Civil Government in the main Estimates amounting to $95,082.50 which were omitted from the figures of this magazine. Other items omitted for this year are Health of Animals, $190,000; Fumigation Stations,

4,000; Foreign Exhibitions, $240,000; a grant of $50,000 for the Dominion Exhibition at Winnipeg; and appropriation for National Live Stock Records, $5,000. In the Estimates of 1910-11, there was omitted under the head of Civil Government $195,653.32, as well as $50,000 under Health of Animals. Now, as I stated a moment ago, every page of this magazine contains inaccuracies quite as glaring and as inexcusable. It does seem extraordinary that a magazine bearing the imprint of the Government and intended to be quoted by the newspapers, and containing the minister's photograph as well as those of of other ministers, should contain such inaccuracies. We have the assurance of the minister that ' to know what others have accomplished; to know their methods of work, to learn the reasons for their successes and failures, is to broaden our own sympathies and to stimulate our own enthusiasm.' In view of that, I should have thought the minister would endeavour to put before the reading public of the Dominion of Canada, and especially before the farmers, a correct summary giving an accurate idea of what others have done for agriculture before the time when he himself assumed the office which he holds at the present time.

I do not wish to take up much time in answering my hon. friend (Mr. Kyte). I do not think it was necessary for my hon. friend to take quite the tone he has taken. He assumes that I deliberately set to work to publish this magazine, not in the interests of agriculture, but directly in the interests of the Conservative Federal Department of Agriculture. I must disclaim anything of that kind. If he knows anything of newspaper work, he knows that a minister who is engaged in supervising and running a fairly large department cannot undertake to read the proofs and verify the information in a magazine of that kind. I can only say that if there are inaccuracies-and I have no doubt that it may be that there will be inaccuracies - these will be very quickly set right. The item of $700,000 on page 62 should not, so far as I can see, have been repeated, but I do not think anybody could have been misled by that. With regard to my hon. friend's items, I do not see that the figures for 1910-11 or for the subsequent year are omitted. The gentleman I put in charge of this work was not placed in the Civil Service by myself; he worked under the Hon. Sydney Fisher, and I believe him to
be a thoroughly capable and thoroughly reliable man who has no political axe to grind. So far as any instructions I have given are concerned, they have been directed to ensuring that all the information published in this magazine is correct, fair and clear. So far as my trying to make political capital out of anything of this kind is-concerned, I have never failed in this-House or on any platform in the country to state in the most absolute and frank way that when my predecessor initiated any work for the benefit of agriculture in this country I did not hesitate to recognize it, and, so far as it was considered to be good, to try to carry it on and expand it. I do not want to take a mean or narrow view of this;.
I do think my hon. friend is very much beside the mark in the tone of his criticism. A large portion of the information published in this magazine is derived from the various-officers of the provincial governments, including the Liberal Government which my hon. friend supports, and if he will read the-next number of the magazine, which is now on the press, he will see a reference there very different in tone from the remarks which the hon. gentleman has made to this committee. The article is from the provincial secretary of agriculture, who looks at this matter from a somewhat broader aspect than my hon. friend does, and who recognizes that we. are making a fair and honest attempt to do something in the interests-of agriculture, regardless of party. While it may appear that we are boosting ourselves politically-the hon. gentleman does not want me to leave out of the magazine everything this Government has done-I think I can say with absolute truth that I am trying to meet in as fair and frank a way as I can the needs of the situation, and to publish this magazine, regardless of polities, in what I believe to be the best interests of agriculture. I am obliged to my hon. friend for having pointed out any inaccuracies, and I shall be very glad if he or any other member of the House will call attention to any mistakes in this magazine, as the sole object we have in view is to give a fair reflection of both Dominion and provincial agricultural activities, for the benefit of all the farmers in the country.

I am obliged to my hon.
friend the Minister of Agriculture for the certificate he furnishes of my adherence to the Liberal Government of the province of - No.va Scotia. I may point out that the information supplied by the Liberal Government of Nova Scotia which appears in this magazine is correct, and that

the information supplied toy the Government at Ottawa is absolutely incorrect. I could, I suppose, have gone to the hon. minister privately, and intimated that I had discovered Some grave inaccuracies in his publication, but I do not think I have exceeded my right in calling public attention to the matter in this way. The hon. minister very properly says that the actual supervision of this work can not be chargeable to him, and that he is not responsible for its inaccuracies. I quite agree with him in that, but strange things are being done, not only in the Department of Agriculture but in every department of this Government, since it came into power. Whether or not they have changed their subordinates I do not know, but I do know that things are not done in many of the departments at the present moment as they have done in the past. Advance notices of Supplementary Estimates, for instance, were not given by the late Government in counties where byelections were about to be held, as was done in the counties of Antigonish and Victoria in the province of Nova Scotia within the last year. That was brought to the attention of	the	Minister of
Public Works last year, and be disclaimed any knowledge of the information having been given out, but a gentleman by the name of Buskard who, I understand, is the minister's private secretary, was the handy man who gave the information for the purpose of influencing the vote in the county of Antigonish a year ago. Further investigation as to the source of information which Tory politicians had as to the votes which were to be passed in this House for the county of Victoria will disclose the fact that the Minister of Public Works' handy man, Mr. Buskard, gave out information beforehand to influence the electors in that constituency. I say, therefore, that while the ministers themselves disclaim any knowledge or responsibility, they appear to have introduced a system of exploitation of the public service which has been unknown in the past, and the sooner the people of this country are brought face to face with a knowledge of the facts, the better it will be for the country, as well as for the ministers themselves.

The assertion that these are only inaccuracies is, in my judgment, altogether too mild. It is a case of glaring misrepresentation, and I think the hon. minister will come to that conclusion if he looks carefully through the publica-

tion. The man who prepared that statement, I care not who he is, is unfit to prepare anything. If he thinks it is correct, he is not qualified for the work; if he knows it to be wrong, that is still worse. I know he is not fit to edit a publication of this kind, and I will give you the proof. In addition to what the minister, and I think, the hon. member for Richmond, (Mr. Kyte) called inaccuracies, I find, under the appropriations for 1899-1900, that the sum of $175,000 for the Paris Exposition, which can be found in the main estimates, was omitted. How that item could have escaped the attention of any man in the Department of Agriculture who was preparing a publication of this kind, I am quite at a loss to understand. Is there not more than an inaccuracy? According to this publication the total amount appropriated by the late Government in the year J899-1900 was $271,000; I find that the total amount appropriated that year was $594,762. In other words, $323,762 were left out, or 120 per cent more left out than were put in. Could that be called an inaccuracy? I do not think so. All these mistakes, or the major portion of them, have reference to the years during which the late Government had the management of the Department of Agriculture. According to this publication the appropriations for the Department of Agriculture in 1904-5 amounted to $388,000, and the correct appropriation for that year was $972,082, this publication being wrong to the extent of $584,082, or 150 per cent.
Mr. -BURRELL: The hon. member is aware, of course, that several branches have been taken out of the Department of Agriculture, and this list is only what pertains to agriculture proper.

I am giving the
items of civil government under the heading of agriculture. In 1911-12, 1912-13 and 1913-14 you include that.

I will not speak positively, but in this list for civil government, as my hon. friend knows, a very large spending department, that of the Census, which has gone out of the Department oL Agriculture, is not included. Those things not relating to agriculture are not put in. My hon. friend referred to leaving out the Paris exhibition. I fancy he will find that no exhibition work is included here. I might have put in a very large amount in connection with the San Francisco and Ghent exhibitions, but

my recollection is that we have not put these in, but have simply put in what relates to Canadian agriculture.

I see under the
head of Dominion grants to exhibitions $200,000 for 1913-14.
I do not see it; I only see $50,000.

Oh, yes, $50,000; that
is right.

Hear, hear.
Mr.	HUGHES:	My	hon. friends	applaud very quickly. But under the late Government $50,000 was expended on the Winnipeg exhibition, and that is left out of this publication. Was it because it was expended under the late Government? Will my hon. friends applaud now?

I see it is in 1910-11. I
do not know why it is left out in the other year.
Mr.	HUGHES:	But	not in the	year
i am referring to.
Mr.	BURRELL:	My	hon. friend	was
speaking of the Paris and some other exhibitions. , I think all those big exhibition votes were left out because they were not considered to relate directly to agriculture.
Why was the vote for the Winnipeg exhibition left out in 1904-05?

I do not know.
Mr.	HUGHES:	The	information	contained in this publication has doubtless been published by a great many of the agricultural papers in this country. I see here the minister says:
Without the assistance of the press the wide dissemination of knowledge would be impossible, and to its members we trust this publication will be of use.
In view of the facts that have been brought to the minister's attention to-night, does he really think the publication is of any proper use to the press of the country?

I am bound to say
that I think it will be of very great use. I think my hon. friend has not a very good sense of proportion. I am not disputing that there may be inaccuracies. Surely my ,hon. friend does not mean to say that the inaccuracies mentioned, which are not very grave and can be easily removed, have a political aspect? He does not mean to say that for that reason all the information in this book, dealing with every province,
giving a historical resume of agriculture and education is to be chucked by the board because of one or two errors that my hon. friend thinks have political significance. I think he is taking a small view.
I cannot agree with him and I do not think the country will agree with him.

That is the worst
feature of this case. He says there are only one or two mistakes and there are more mistakes than there are entries in those years. In 1900 there are five items left out altogether that ought to be in and there are not many more put in. The amounts left out are larger than the amounts put in. The next period there are eight entries for very large amounts left out. In 1905-00 main Estimates item 55, on page 35, $100,000 for the health of animals is left out; Supplementary Estimates, item 22, page 4, $50,000; Supplementary Estimates, item 30, page 4, $40,000 left out. Foreign exhibitions I shall leave out because the minister says he has not put them in under the other headings. That is the year that the exhibition grant at Winnipeg, $50,000,- is left out; National Livestock Record, Supplementary Estimates, item 4, page 4, $5,000 left out. Those are only one or two of the inaccuracies.

If we want to show the gradual development of agriculture and its encouragement by the federal Government -and surely it is a good thing to develop agriculture-it is a good plan to show the amounts that have been expended. The hon. member will admit that figures in the main are accurate.

I want the minister to
understand that this publication is entirely misleading and improper. If the minister will admit that something will have been accomplished.
I cannot admit that.

That would be admitting what is a fact, and if he would say that he would withdraw it or in the next publication call attention to the misrepresentations or inaccuracies that are contained in this publication, it would help to remedy the evil. If the minister is going to give information at all he ought to give correct information.

Let me assure my hon. friend, who I do not think wants to be unfair, that I am not animated by any other considerations; and I would be very glad to have the corrections made. It could not be done in this number because I think it

is now in the printer's hands, but in the March number any substantial errors that are pointed out I will be glad to have corrected. I have no other wish than to do what is fair. The hon. member is holding me up as a very demon of political iniquity. He thinks I am inspiring all these things, when I know I will be subject to criticism and rightly so, unless the information is honestly and fairly set out. The hon. gentleman never yet saw the first number of any paper or magazine, a new venture, that did not contain some mistakes. I am afraid that he is holding me responsible to too great a degree.
If there were only a few mistakes there would be some excuse.
None of us are infallible, not even the youngest.

When the mistakes
are so glaring and prominent and amount to so much, and when they all happen to be in the period during which the late Government had charge of the Agriculture Department, it cannot but strike one as a peculiar feature in connection with the publication of this Gazette.

Suppose we take it for granted that the Minister is in earnest over his publication. I find that the first number is devoted to a description of the work done at the Experimental Farms; the work of the cereal division and the chemistry division is explained. Will the other numbers be on the same line, or will they deal with agricultural education proper, that is, the feeding of pigs, the growing of crops, and things of that kind? While I appreciate the Minister's efforts to give information to the public, I think that this paper, if it is to be any good, should get into the hands of the farmers, and merely telling them that you have a poultry division and a cereal division and things of that sort will not be of much benefit to the ordinary farmer. The mere fact of sending this pamphlet to members of Parliament, three-quarters of whom are not farmers, will not benefit the farming community. It is much on the same principle of sending a Patent Record to me, it would be absolutely useless. I looked through this pamphlet carefully for any information such as I might find in a farmers' magazine, but I did not find any.
I am not finding fault at all. If there are mistakes in this first number, I take it for granted that the Minister is absolutely truthful when he says he did not know of 
these mistakes. Still, as his name appears on the second page, he should have had some supervision over the contents. His name appearing like that, is a guarantee of the truthfulness of the pamphlet, and he should have been a little more careful, I think, in looking over the proof sheets. I would like to know what is his ultimate object, whether these pamphlets are to be given to the farmers or to members of Parliament?

I am sorry I have not fuller information about this. I did not expect this magazine question to come up to-night, because it is largely associated with a vote taken under the Agricultural Instruction Act, and is not very closely associated with the vote we are now discussing. When I had the idea of this magazine in my mind, I wrote a long letter to every Provincial Minister of Agriculture in Canada, explaining my idea; that I thought it was time for Canada to follow in the wake of every progressive country and have an official magazine of organized agriculture. I asked them to express their opinions, and told them that we were trying to avoid that criticism which has perhaps justly been made of all governments, that government publications take such a long time to get out that the press and the people do not get at the results of the work that is being carried on. It was partly with the idea of meeting that criticism that we issued this magazine, giving monthly a brief statement of agri-cunural and research work, and items of scientific and practical interest in connection with the departmental work here and all over Canada. My' hon. friend will understand that you cannot judge any publication by Its first number, or even by its second. Rome was not built in a day. The magazine is prepared with the idea of giving a general survey of agricultural conditions in Canada. We will welcome the suggestions of any hon. member for making this publication better, because I think a work of this kind should go on, no matter whether this Government is in power or any other Government.
Will the minister publish the correct tables in the March number that should have been published in this number?
We shall be very glad to make any corrections.

This discussion reminds me of a certain gentleman who com-

plained to a newspaper editor about certain things he had printed about him. The editor said: ' My dear sir, if you could only see the things I did not print about you, you would not complain.' I think the hon. gentlemen opposite, instead of criticising this first number, should congratulate themselves upon what has been kept out of it. For instance, there might have appeared in that issue the statement which the former Minister of Agriculture, Hon. Sydney Fisher, made in the session of 1909, to the effect that the farmers of Canada were a lazy, slipshod and indifferent class of people. I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will not complain that the editor was kind enough to omit that. I must say, of course, that it would be extremely interesting reading to the farmers.

When did he make that
statement?

You will find it in
' Hansard ' of the session of 1909. I will get the exact page for you later. This magazine might also have referred to the statement of the former Minister of Agriculture in answer to a question that I put him in 1909, that for the 10 years previous to 1909 the Liberal party had only expended a little over $6,000,000 in the interests of agriculture, or an average of $604,000 a year. Hon. gentlemen opposite will not complain that that was omitted. I repeat that hon. gentlemen opposite should feel grateful because of the things that have been left out of this publication. If we were to go into details of what was not done under the former Government in the interests of agriculture, we could not hope to get it in one issue of the magazine, or in one issue of the papers published in the city of Ottawa. The omissions are legion. What did they do in the fifteen years they were in power in the interest of agriculture? Lei them point out anything that they did. They made promises previous to 1896 of what they were going to do, but they did not carry out a single promise that they made? If you take the consensus of opinion from one end of Canada to the other amongst the farmers, they will say that this present Government, in the two years they have been in office, have done more in the interest of agriculture than the Liberal party did in the whole fifteen years they were "in power.

I think it will be found that what the Hon. Mr. Fisher did state was that the farmers of Canada, if a great
many of them did not farm in a miserable, slipshod manner, could raise a good deal more stuff on their farms than they do. I rather think that that statement was absolutely true and that the present Minister of Agriculture will agree with it. If he does not, he does not know much about what the farmers in Canada are doing. 1, as a farmer, am quite free to say that if it were not for the slipshod manner in which some farmers carry on their farming operations, they could vastly increase their production. I am not finding any fault with my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture for omitting from these pages some of the items that were devoted to agriculture, because I am not one of those who think that the Government gain so much as they probably think they do by what they call the expenditure on agriculture. The farmers, as far as I know them, are not asking for pap feed; they are asking for an open and free market and cheap transportation. The farmers in my section of the country are absolutely capable of managing their own affairs and giving themselves largely their own education. They are able to compete with any other farmers in the world if they have free markets and are able to sell to the highest markets. I think my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has quoted the Hon. Mr. Fisher improperly when he simply puts in a few words without telling what the discussion was about.

I do not think any one has taken the exception with reference to the item now under discussion, that there has been anything left out in the past except regarding that amount. It is for the year 1899-1900 and also for the year 1904-1905. That item is given in full. I take the view that instead of criticising the minister as you have been doing, you ought to give him credit for having given the Estimates for the last two years the late Government were in power when the Estimates were higher than they were at any time previous to that. No exception has been taken to the Estimates given during these two years. I was a little surprised that the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) could not get any information from this pamphlet. I did think, a few weeks ago, when he was speaking on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, that he was sadly lacking in such information as he could find in such a pamphlet as we have here. I notice here that the manner is stated in which the grant under the Act for aid to agriculture

is expended in each of the various provinces. With reference to the province of Ontario, the province from which the hon. gentleman comes, if I remember rightly, in speaking on the Address, he said: Who knows anything about how this money has been expended ? I have addressed gatherings up in my riding and I have asked the question: Where has this money gone ? If the hon. gentleman had just looked here he would have found that his own district, and those districts to which he 11 p.m. referred on that occasion, are provided for out of this amount, because he will find that of the $195,000 paid to the province of Ontario, $80,000 was paid for district representatives. He also complained that nothing was being done to encourage agriculture in the public schools; yet, he will find by looking through this pamphlet that there was $10,000 devoted to that purpose. Some of the schools in his own riding received an appropriation for that purpose.
Not one.
I have to differ with my hon. friend.
Name them.
The school on the tenth line of East Zorra.
I asked the people that on the tenth line, and they said not. Do they or you know better?
You did not ask the right people.
I ought to have asked some Tories, I suppose.

I could -point out some more things that he could learn about for which money has been expended, but he did not want to be fair, he did not want to give the provincial government credit for doing anything, and he was trying to belittle this Government and to make it appear that the money that was paid for agriculture was not accomplishing anything in the province of Ontario. I think that some hon. gentlemen opposite are trying to make a mountain out of a molehill, and it is not going to amount to very much after all.
Some of the criticisms that were made by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Ky.te) could be explained away with a little conf.Mr. Sutherland.]
sideration. There is also some very valuable information given in this pamphlet in regard to the item that is now under discussion, and I hope that every hon. member of this House will peruse it carefully. There is information that will be of great value in regard to the amount that is expended for experimental farms and stations. The statement was made that all of these stations, with the exception of three, were established by the late Government. I can only say that I see that provision is made for establishing another one in the province of Quebec that is not included in this list. There are also several others, and I think that when the total is made out it will amount to more than three.
I desire to call the minister's attention to the fact that with the twenty experimental farms, outside of the central farm and the seven sub-stations, there are only forty acres in the province of Ontario devoted to experimental purposes. Of the 6,669 acres in the Dominion of Canada constituting experimental farms, there are only 40 acres in Ontario set apart for this purpose, and this area is devoted, I believe, to experimenting in regard to the production of tobacco. That surely offers food for consideration to the members of this House. We have heard a great deal this afternoon from hon. gentlemen opposite about the lands in western Canada, and how they should be handed over to the provinces. We also heard some hon. gentlemen making the claim that the provinces were receiving greater benefits by leaving these lands with the Dominion Government. When you consider the large amount compared with former years that has been spent for experimental purposes, and when you realize that there are only 40 acres and a very trifling expenditure devoted to experimental purposes in the whole province of Ontario, you will come to the conclusion that some change must be made in this respect and made in the very near future.
I have here a document brought out by the Conservation Commission last year. It contains an address delivered by Professor Fernow of Toronto University, before this commission in the city of Ottawa on the 28th of December last. I do not believe that there was ever a document published by the authority of any commission under any government that did any province in this country so great an injury as that document has done, and it is absolutely necessary for this Government to see that at an early date experimental farms are

established in the northern parts of this province. I could show that the man who delivered that address had not a proper knowledge of the conditions, having simply gone through the country on a four days' trip on the Transcontinental railway and in a motor car. Having done that, he thinks he is in a position to deliver, before the Conservation Commission, an address to be circulated in pamphlet form broadcast throughout this country and making it appear that northern Ontario is a cold, barren, inhospitable country to live in; that it is a frozen country where one is liable to have frost and snow at any season of the year. When I read that address, I was *wondering what the hon. gentlemen from the western provinces would say if such a document was circulated in respect to the western provinces, because the land which Professor Fernow inspected was not nearly as far north as the city of Winnipeg, yet because it is in the province of Ontario, it is anything but desirable. That is the condition under which Ontario is labouring at the present time and has been during all these years.
Ai little experimental farm has been established by the present Administration in the county of Essex. I give the hon. minister credit for doing something, even if it is an experiment with regard to growing tobacco. But there are other things to be done in this province that ought to be done in the very near future.

In answer to my hon.
friend Irom South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) in regard to his reference to me, at every meeting which I attended, I asked the farmers if they had seen any advantage of the money voted for agricultural education. In every instance there was dead silence. I only repeated that and I will repeat it again. My hon. friend says that the Minister of Agriculture by that donation paid the district representatives. I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if that is true, because we had district representatives long before that grant -was made. For several years the province has supplied district representatives in various sections of the country.
You did not have them in the county of Oxford.

No, but in various sections of the country. They were applied for, not to the Dominion Government, but to the provincial Government, and were granted by the provincial Government. The gentleman to whom I referred is a very nice
young fellow, and I do not say anything against him, nor did I say anything against him when I was addressing the House before. I thought he should rather hold classes in the country schools than at the Collegiate institutes. I gave him credit for what he did at the Collegiate institutes. He had a good class there and the young men in his class felt that they were benefited. I tol'd the Minister of Agriculture that this instruction should be extended to the country schools and not left entirely to the city schools. At that time he agreed with me.
As to my stating from this Gazette what was done for agriculture in Ontario at that time, that would have been impossible, because this book was not issued until after that.
All the more reason why you should appreciate the book.

I have said nothing
against the book.	I asked the minister
what the future issues were going to be. If they are to be along the same lines as this, I quite frankly say that I do not believe that there will be any benefit to the agricultural community, 'but if, in the next issues, he intends to give the results of experiments in certain lines of agriculture, the probabilities are that benefits will result if these issues reach the people. There is no object in their being sent to members of Parliament and that class of people, because in that case farmers do not get this information.

I am bound to say with the hon. Minister of Agriculture that I expect .a great deal from this publication, provided it is published in the real interest of the farmers and that there are not to be found any such inaccuracies as were pointed out this evening. I thank the hon. minister for having published this Gazette from the very first number in both languages. The people in Quebec will appreciate that.
Not only are there inaccuracies, which my hon. friend promises to remedy, in the information contained in this Gazette, but i find that some of the answers given by my hon. friend during the course of the session on this very question of exhibitions, international and universal, are inaccurate. I am quite sure that it was inadvertent on the part of my hon. friend that such information was given to the House. For instance, on February 2, I put the following question to my hon. frierfd:
What amount of money has been spent by the federal Government since 1896 for the uni-

versal or international exhibitions which have been held the world over?
My hon. friend's answer was: ' $2,129,132.05.' I took the Auditor General's reports since 1896 and made a general survey, and I found that my hon. friend or an officer in his department had erred by something like $629,118.84. I have here a tabulated statement which gives exactly the figures year by year. I am quite sure that this has escaped the attention of my hon. friend and that it is not his own mistake but the mistake of one of his officials.
Speaking about the expenditure of the Department of Agriculture, I would like to know who in the department of my hon.' friend is the land purchasing agent. I understand that my hon. friend some months ago purchased at Lev;s a site for a quarantine station. I wish to call my hon. friend's attention to this fact that, unless he pays particular attention to his agents in or around Quebec, he will find that the farmers of this country, my hon. friend himself, and the Government of Canada, are being mulcted. Let me give an instance. My hon. friend, in July 1913, bought some lots at Levis for a quarantine station, paying the sum of $32,750. Would he believe me if I tell him, that that very site, had been purchased one year before for $5,500? Is it possible that within a year property in Levis should have advanced at that rate?
What has that to do with this item?

I will tell the hon.
gentleman what it has to do with the farmers of Canada. On the 30th of July, 1913, Mr. W. R. Dohan sold to the Department of Agriculture this site for a quarantine station for $32,750. Four days previous, on July 26, 1913, he had bought this site for $25,400 from a man named Dussault. His profit in four days amounted to $7,250. Dussault, of St. David, had purchased this property one month before, paying for it $12,200, thus within a month and four days a profit of $13,200 had been made out of the Government of Canada. This property had been purchased from one Buteau in July, 1912, eleven months before, for $5,500. Now, is it not fair that the minister should know these facts? He is head of the department which takes special care of the farming interests in Canada. Is it a good thing that the money of the farmers should be squandered for the benefit of land speculators in the city of Levis? I think not; and I know that my hon. friend will look

into these facts and see to it in future that the department and the farmers of Canada are not mulcted for the benefit of land speculators.

I think that one expression which the hon. gentleman dropped towards the close of his remarks goes far to explain the situation-' land speculators.' He knows that for a very long time past we have been in trouble in regard to a quarantine station in Quebec. It was a difficult question to solve, and we have given it a lot of attention. About a year and a half ago we endeavoured to formulate a plan to secure the necessary land. We found the prices of land going up every day, and we could not deal. Finally, I did get word of the property to which he refers and I sent the Veterinary Director General down, and he, in consultation with Mr. Couture, whom the hon. gentleman knows, went into the whole case. It is very important to the stock raisers in Canada to get satisfactory quarantine ground in Quebec where so much of the stock is landed. After a reputable citizen of Quebec-whose name I have forgotten at the moment, but which the committee can learn of from the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier)-had given a value on this property, and after a very careful examination to make sure that it was suitable for our purposes, after reports not only by the Director General but also by Mr. Drisdale, the Director of Experimental Farms-a man not appointed by me, but by my predecessor, as my hon. friend knows-which reports and investigation showed that the property was more admirably suited for our purpose than any other in the district, we concluded that we were justified in buying it. I do not know the facts as to the previous transactions except as given by my hon. friend. It is quite possible that a year ago the property was not worth half the money. But I have seen cases in the West, as I am sure he has seen them in the East, of property that has gone up ten and twenty times in a year, by reasons of some element of speculation entering in. So far as the depart-iment is concerned, we were absolutely careful to see that the property for our purposes was worth the money and that it was more suitable than any other for our purpose of safeguarding the live-stock of Canada.

As my hon. friend
and colleague has referred to me, I wish to tell the part which I took

in this matter. On one occasion whilst in Quebec on business, I received a telegram from my colleague informing me that a property was offered him for the purpose of a quarantine station and asking me if I could give information as to the value. I was not able to go to Levis to visit the property, but suggested that a man should be engaged to look at it, a man who is above reproach and is regarded as absolutely honourable and trustworthy by everybody, Mr. Audet, a notary of Levis. I told my colleague that whatever Mr. Audet reported he could depend upon. I do not know the property myself, but know in a general way where it is situated. I understand that Mr. Audet investigated the matter and sent the valuation to my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture.

The hon. minister is
well versed in real estate in and around Quebec. Would he say that a piece of property in Levis bought in July, 1912, for $5,500 could be worth in 1913 the sum of $32,750?

I am not surprised
at that at all. Property has increased in Levis and Quebec to a very great extent. I do not know the figures in this case, but I can tell the hon. gentleman the property purchased within the last two or three years in Levis or Quebec could not be purchased to-day except at a very great advance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid hon. gentlemen are wandering a little from the item under discussion. We are now dealing with item number 44, experimental farms.

Will the hon. minister
explain the increases there?

It is to provide for a general extension of the. whole system of experimental farms, and for dealing with any new properties we may have to acquire in any part of the country. I need not tell my hon. friend, who is familiar with the whole farm system, that the work is growing in every branch. For instance, at the central farm the expansion has been very great, and we are very much crowded for room. Within the last few years we have adpoted a system that is different from the old one. We have specialists who are carrying on, in connection with the central farm, a series of experiments in connection with various lines of agricultural research at all the farms. In Ottawa, where we used to have the live-stock industry and the field husbandry carried on under one officer, Mr. Grisdale, we have now a separate live stock branch, under the direction of Mr. Archibald, who came from Nova Scotia, and a separate man in charge of the husbandry. We have also additional specialists in fodders and grasses. All this is very valuable work. If, after long research and experiment, we find that certain things are of great value to the farmer, when that information filters down to the man operating the farm, it may make all the difference in the world between his profit and loss when he comes to carry out the suggestions that are made.

How do you get that
information to the farmer?

Of course it is got to
the farmer in a great many ways. It is got to the farmer through lectures delivered by various provincial agents; through the publications of the department, of which we now issue nearly two million, having greatly increased the list. These publications, though it is possible that some persons do not read them, are read with great interest and profit all through Canada. Through such agencies as the Gazette we are publishing, and in a number of other ways, this information goes perhaps not directly to the farmer, but ultimately does get to those interested. The information may go, for instance, to the Macdonald school, to the schools at Guelph, Truro or to those which are established in Alberta at the present time, and through these agencies the information is communicated to hundreds and thousands of people whom we could not reach. So that in the end my hon. friend will see that the information filters down to a great many people whom it is very necessary to reach, if they are to get the help in their work that they certainly wish to get.	So far as	we are
concerned, it is our business to try to give that information to those interested in such a way as to help them in their work. If I had time it would not be difficult to prove that in spite of drawbacks and in spite of some things which have been the subject of, perhaps fair criticism, the general work of the experimental farms is doing much for Canada and for Canadian agriculture. I would almost say that we are ahead of any other country so far as the research and investigation and experimental work that has been, carried on in Canada is concerned. The present system was inaugurated in 1886 by Sir John Carling, it was carried forward and expanded under my predecessors, and we are carry-
ing it further forward. I hope that we will be able further to improve it, and that we will have the support of everybody in trying to ^mprove and expand it.

This agricultural Gazette
tells us that the department has two experimental dairy stations, one at Finch, making cheese and butter, and another at Brome making butter. Would the minister tell the committee if the experimental station at Brome is making butter at the present time, and where that butter is being shipped to?

I am afraid that I could not give my hon. friend the details of every item offhand. I may say, however, that I shall be glad to give him that information when we come to deal with the item of dairy work.

In order to give the minister an opportunity of making a fair statement with regard to the matter, I think I should tell him to-night the position I hold because of representations made to me by people who are patrons of this particular creamery. I am told that they are not making butter in that creamery, that it is run now as a skimming station, that the cream is sold to a man named Olmstead at Sutton, and that Mr. Olmstead is shipping this cream partly to the United States.

I shall be glad to get
my hon. friend all the information he requires. I am not afraid to say that the work carried on in this respect by Mr. Ruddick meets with the approval of everybody. I am sure my hon. friends opposite found Mr. Ruddick to he a very competent man, who has the entire confidence of the dairy men throughout the country, and I am confident that the experimental work carried on under him in that regard must be accomplishing some good.

I would suggest to my
hon. friend leading the Opposition that the committee rise and report progress.
This is an important item, and seems to be attracting a good deal of attention. Perhaps we might pass a smaller item and let this one stand.
I shall be glad to come back to the item at any time.

One of the questions I
wish to ask the minister is what results are being obtained from experiments with Prelude wheat.

I hope my hon. friend will not hesitate to come back to the item

after it is passed; I think it is only fair, and I shall be very glad to give him any information he may require.
Perhaps the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), who is now in his seat, will give the quotation to which reference has been made.

I quote, from 'Hansard ' of March 3, 1900, pp. 1963 and 1964, the following words used by Hon. Sydney Fisher, then Minister of Agriculture:
It is tlie farmer's slipshod methods in this country which is the limit of our agricultural production. The only pity is that the farmers of Canada are not doubling and quadrupling their exports every year. If they do not do it, it is not for lack of teaching or lack of knowledge ; it is for their lack of interest in their work, their lack of industry, and largely, I believe, for the lack of that labour which is necessary in the carrying on of our farming operations.
The assertion that there is lack of interest in their work is a charge of indifference.

Many of them are indifferent.
y Mr. EDWARDS:	That would apply to a
great many who are not farmers.
They are nearly as bad as members of Parliament.

And when it charges
them with a lack of industry I presume I am right in interpreting that as an accusation of laziness-
-and largely for the lack of that labour which is necessary in the carrying on of our farming operations.
I say that in not one of these particulars was the then Minister of Agriculture justified in charging the farmers of Ontario, as he did, with indifference, laziness and a general lack of interest in their particular vocation, because I claim that if you examine into the record of agricultural production in Canada and compare it with that of agricultural production in other countries you will find that those words cannot be truthfully applied to the farmers . of this country, and that when the minister at that time was placing that blame upon the shoulders of the farmers and at the same time declaring that he, as Minister of Agriculture, had furnished them with all the knowledge and facilities they required, he was simply trying to unload his own defects as minister upon the shoulders of the farmers whom he had not properly served as minister. I say he was not

warranted in making the statement that he *did, that agricultural production in this country gave the lie to every charge he made against the farmers of the country, and that he, as Minister of Agriculture, himself presuming to be a farmer, was the last man who should have made that charge. I call attention to that as one of the things which I presume those who got up this Gazette were aware of and out of a kindness of their hearts had refrained from placing on the record.

(Translation.)-I am somewhat surprised at the zeal displayed by the hon. gentlemen opposite, who voted, when in power, a few hundred thousand dollars only, for agricultural purposes, whilst the present government is now spending $3,950,000 for the same object.
The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) is amazed by the great increase in value of the property around Quebec; let me tell him that coming, as he does, from the province of Quebec, he should not wonder. It is true that, when his party was in power, Quebec felt satisfied with the the sole mention of the name of the then Premier, who has done nothing for their city; and there lays the reason why Quebec and its neighbourhood did not grow as it does to-day.
We have now in the Postmaster General a man who has taken so much interest in Quebec's, and its surroundings, welfare, that property valuated, one year ago, at $5,500 is to-day sold for $32,000. This is due to the fact that during the last few years Quebec and its surroundings have taken such an increase, that property, in the neighbourhood, will reach unforeseen high prices, and the ex-Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) must not be looking for a stumbling-block, which does not exist.
We have in the Postmaster General a man who has taken Quebec's welfare to heart.
Progress reported.
